title: India Launches $15 Billion Semiconductor Push to Build Chip Fabrication Ecosystem
excerpt: With 12 approved projects, three facilities already in production, and a roadmap to 3nm chip manufacturing, India is positioning itself as a credible alternative in the global semiconductor supply chain.
body:
• India has approved 12 semiconductor projects worth over Rs 1.64 lakh crore ($19.7 billion), with three facilities already in commercial production.
  • The Semicon 2.0 program, with an outlay of Rs 1.27 lakh crore ($15.3 billion), targets advanced chip fabrication down to 2nm and 3nm nodes.
  • Tata Electronics' fab plant in Dholera, Gujarat — India's first chip fabrication facility — has received formal SEZ notification, while Micron has begun commercial production at its Sanand assembly plant.
  • The government aims to manufacture chips meeting 70-75% of domestic demand by 2029, with the Indian semiconductor market projected to reach $100-110 billion by 2030.

A Second-Phase Semiconductor Bet

India has moved decisively from semiconductor ambition to execution. The government has launched Semicon 2.0 with a Cabinet-approved outlay of Rs 1.27 lakh crore ($15.3 billion), building on the first phase's Rs 76,000 crore allocation. Together, 12 semiconductor projects with investment commitments exceeding Rs 1.64 lakh crore have been approved, and three facilities have already entered commercial production.

https://x.com/BJP4India/status/2087873706861498760

The program targets the full value chain: chip design, fabrication, advanced packaging, semiconductor equipment and materials, research and development, and talent. Semicon 2.0 includes a defined roadmap for achieving 3nm and 2nm technology nodes — a significant escalation from the first phase, which focused primarily on getting basic manufacturing capability off the ground.

"The first phase was about getting manufacturing capability off the ground. The second one is broader: design, fabs, packaging, materials, equipment, R&D and talent, all at once."

— Saurabh Agarwal, Partner, EY India

Projects Taking Shape on the Ground

The most visible progress is at Micron Technology's assembly and test facility in Sanand, Gujarat, which has begun commercial production and shipped its first made-in-India memory modules to Dell Technologies. Micron expects to assemble tens of millions of chips at Sanand in 2026, scaling to hundreds of millions by 2027.

Meanwhile, Tata Electronics' chip fabrication plant at Dholera, Gujarat — a joint venture with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation — has received formal Special Economic Zone notification. The facility spans over 66 hectares and is expected to create roughly 21,000 jobs, making it India's first true chip fabrication plant. Kaynes Semicon and CG Power, in partnership with Japan's Renesas Electronics, are also developing packaging and assembly facilities.

In Odisha, 3D Glass Solutions broke ground on an advanced chip packaging unit in Bhubaneswar, while India has pursued Dutch semiconductor expertise, with a trade delegation visiting Eindhoven to court suppliers in the ASML ecosystem. Applied Materials, the world's second-largest chipmaking equipment maker, has committed $400 million to R&D operations in India.

A Differentiated Strategy

Industry experts argue India's path is not about replicating Taiwan or South Korea in advanced logic fabrication, but carving a distinct niche. India's competitive advantages lie in its deep pool of chip design talent, growing domestic demand, strong government backing, and its position as a trusted partner for supply chain diversification.

"India's strongest competitive edge lies not in immediately matching Taiwan, South Korea, or China in advanced chip fabrication, but in building a differentiated semiconductor ecosystem," Krishan Arora, Partner at Grant Thornton Bharat, told the Times of India.

The domestic semiconductor market stood at roughly $38 billion in 2023 and is projected to reach $100-110 billion by 2030, according to industry estimates. The government's target is for India to design and manufacture chips covering 70-75% of its domestic requirements by 2029.

Challenges Remain

Semiconductor fabrication is capital-intensive with long development cycles, and India's ecosystem remains heavily service-oriented rather than product-led. Commercialization — turning design talent into globally competitive semiconductor businesses — is the critical gap, according to Shivani Parashar of Counterpoint Research.

"The missing piece is converting India's engineering talent into globally successful semiconductor businesses," Parashar said, adding that India needs a stronger venture capital ecosystem capable of supporting 7-10 year development cycles and multiple tape-outs.

EY's Agarwal cautioned that fabs draw attention, but the harder work lies in building out equipment manufacturing, specialty materials, gases and chemicals, research infrastructure, and a skilled workforce. "A few years ago, semiconductors in India were mostly a talking point. That's changed. We now have real projects on the ground," he said. "But that's just a starting point to a long road."
